Status flags, Shifter, Complementer, and Arithmetic and Boolean logic
questions.explanationEn: Figure 14.2 (Slide 3.11, p. 6) illustrates the internal structure of the CPU: the ALU contains Status flags, Shifter, Complementer, and Arithmetic and Boolean logic, all communicating with Registers and the Control Unit across the Internal CPU bus.

questions.subtopic: User-Visible vs. Control and Status Registers
questions.concept: User-Visible Registers vs. Control and Status Registers
questions.question: According to Slide 3.12 ('Register Organization', p. 7), how are CPU registers classified into two primary roles, and which registers belong to each role?
options: (1) User-visible registers (General Purpose, Data, Address, Condition Codes) enable assembly programmers to minimize main memory references; and (2) Control and status registers (PC, IR, MAR, MBR) are used by the control unit and privileged OS programs to control execution
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.12 divides processor registers into: (1) User-visible registers (General Purpose, Data, Address, Condition Role) used by machine/assembly programmers to minimize main memory references, and (2) Control and status registers (PC, IR, MAR, MBR) used by the control unit and privileged OS programs.
questions.explanationVi: Slide 3.12 (trang 7) phân loại thanh ghi thành 2 nhóm: (1) Thanh ghi hiển thị với người lập trình (User-visible registers: Đa năng, Dữ liệu, Địa chỉ, Mã điều kiện) giúp giảm truy cập bộ nhớ chính; và (2) Thanh ghi điều khiển và trạng thái (Control and status registers: PC, IR, MAR, MBR) dùng bởi khối điều khiển và Hệ điều hành.

questions.concept: Architectural milestones of Intel 8086, 8087, 8088, 80286, and 80386
questions.question: Compare the Intel 8086 (1979), 80286 (1982), and 80386 (1985) processors based on Slides 3.13–3.14: which processor introduced Protected Mode with 16 MB addressable memory, and which processor first defined the 32-bit IA-32 architecture with 4 GB addressable memory, paging, and the flat memory model?
options: The 8086 introduced 32-bit registers and 4 GB memory; the 80286 introduced 64-bit registers
The 8088 was a 32-bit processor with a floating-point unit on-chip; the 80386 only supported 1 MB of memory
Protected Mode and Paging were first introduced on the Pentium 4 in 2000

The 80286 introduced Protected Mode and a 24-bit address bus (2^24 = 16 MB); the 80386 was the first 32-bit processor to define the IA-32 architecture with a 32-bit address bus (2^32 = 4 GB), paging, virtual memory, and the flat memory model (where segmentation can be turned off)
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.13–3.14 state: 8086 (1979) had 16-bit registers, 16-bit data bus, 20-bit address bus (1 MB), and real-address mode segmentation (64 KB segments), with 8087 as the FPU co-processor and 8088 using an 8-bit data bus. 80286 (1982) had a 24-bit address bus (16 MB) and introduced Protected Mode. 80386 (1985) was the first 32-bit processor (IA-32), with 32-bit data/address buses (4 GB), introducing paging, virtual memory, and the flat memory model.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.13–3.14: Chip 80286 (1982) có bus địa chỉ 24-bit (16 MB) và giới thiệu Chế độ bảo vệ (Protected mode); Chip 80386 (1985) là bộ xử lý 32-bit đầu tiên định nghĩa kiến trúc IA-32 với bus địa chỉ/dữ liệu 32-bit (4 GB), giới thiệu kỹ thuật phân trang (paging), bộ nhớ ảo và mô hình bộ nhớ phẳng (flat memory model).

questions.concept: Innovations in Intel P6 Family (Pentium Pro, II, III) and Pentium 4
questions.question: According to Slides 3.15–3.16, what key microarchitectural features were introduced in the **Pentium Pro (1995)**, **Pentium II (1997)**, **Pentium III (1999)**, and **Pentium 4 (2000 / 2002)**?
options: Pentium Pro introduced 4-bit registers; Pentium II introduced real-mode segmentation; Pentium 4 removed all caches
Pentium III introduced the 80-bit x87 FPU stack; Pentium Pro only addressed 1 MB of RAM

Pentium Pro: 3-way superscalar, 36-bit address bus (64 GB), dynamic (out-of-order/speculative) execution, on-chip 256 KB L2 cache; Pentium II: MMX instructions; Pentium III: SSE instructions and eight 128-bit XMM registers; Pentium 4: NetBurst deep pipeline, SSE2, and Hyper-Threading (2002, running 2 programs simultaneously sharing resources)
Hyper-Threading was introduced in 1979 on the 8086 processor
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.15–3.16 detail: Pentium Pro (1995) was 3-way superscalar, had a 36-bit address bus (64 GB), introduced dynamic execution (out-of-order and speculative execution), and integrated a 256 KB L2 cache. Pentium II (1997) added MMX. Pentium III (1999) added SSE and eight 128-bit XMM registers. Pentium 4 (2000) introduced Intel NetBurst, SSE2, and in 2002 Hyper-Threading technology.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.15–3.16: Pentium Pro (1995) có kiến trúc siêu vô hướng bậc 3 (3-way superscalar), bus địa chỉ 36-bit (64 GB), thực thi động (out-of-order & speculative) và tích hợp 256 KB L2 cache; Pentium II thêm tập lệnh MMX; Pentium III thêm tập lệnh SSE và 8 thanh ghi 128-bit XMM; Pentium 4 dùng vi kiến trúc NetBurst, SSE2 và công nghệ siêu phân luồng Hyper-Threading (2002).

questions.concept: Pentium-M, EM64T, and IA-32e Mode
questions.question: What enhancements did Intel's **Extended Memory 64-bit Technology (EM64T, 2004)** and **IA-32e Mode** introduce compared to 32-bit IA-32 (Slides 3.17–3.18)?
options: EM64T reduced the number of registers from 8 to 4 and limited physical RAM to 640 KB

EM64T increased the number of general-purpose registers from 8 to 16, widened GPRs and pointers to 64 bits, expanded physical address space up to 2^40 = 1 Terabyte, and provided IA-32e Mode comprising a Compatibility Mode (for legacy 16- and 32-bit applications) and 64-bit Mode (using 64-bit addresses and operands)
IA-32e Mode cannot run 32-bit applications without recompiling the hardware
Pentium-M was a high-power server chip that ran at 10 GHz with no L2 cache
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.17–3.18 state that EM64T (2004) is a 64-bit superset of IA-32: 64-bit GPRs and pointers, number of GPRs increased from 8 to 16, physical address space up to 2^40 = 1 TB. IA-32e Mode includes Compatibility mode (for legacy 16- and 32-bit apps) and 64-bit Mode (64-bit addresses and operands).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.17–3.18: Công nghệ EM64T (2004) mở rộng kiến trúc IA-32 lên 64-bit, tăng số thanh ghi đa năng (GPR) từ 8 lên 16 thanh ghi 64-bit, mở rộng không gian địa chỉ vật lý lên tới 2^40 = 1 TB. Chế độ IA-32e bao gồm Compatibility mode (chạy ứng dụng 16/32-bit cũ) và 64-bit Mode.

questions.concept: Specialized uses of IA-32 General-Purpose Registers
questions.question: In the IA-32 architecture (Slide 3.21), besides general arithmetic and data movement, what are the specialized hardware roles of `EAX`, `ECX`, `ESP`, `ESI`/`EDI`, and `EBP`?
options: EAX: Stack Pointer; ECX: Instruction Pointer; ESP: Loop Counter; EBP: Floating-Point Accumulator
ESI and EDI store segment descriptors; EAX stores the EFLAGS bits

EAX: Accumulator (automatically used by multiplication and division instructions); ECX: Counter (automatically used by LOOP instructions); ESP: Stack Pointer (used by PUSH/POP, points to top of stack); ESI/EDI: Source/Destination Index (used by string instructions); EBP: Base Pointer (references parameters and local variables on the stack)
All eight registers are strictly read-only and can only be modified by the BIOS
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.21 lists the exact specialized roles: EAX = Accumulator (multiplication/division), ECX = Counter (LOOP instructions), ESP = Stack Pointer (PUSH/POP, top of stack), ESI/EDI = Source/Destination Index (string instructions), and EBP = Base Pointer (parameters and local variables on the stack).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.21: Các công dụng chuyên biệt của thanh ghi đa năng gồm: `EAX` (Accumulator - dùng tự động trong lệnh nhân/chia), `ECX` (Counter - bộ đếm tự động cho lệnh LOOP), `ESP` (Stack Pointer - trỏ đỉnh stack khi PUSH/POP), `ESI`/`EDI` (Source/Destination Index - dùng cho lệnh xử lý chuỗi), và `EBP` (Base Pointer - truy xuất tham số và biến cục bộ trên stack).

questions.concept: Accessing 32-bit, 16-bit, and 8-bit parts of GPRs in IA-32 vs. x86-64
questions.question: Compare the sub-register naming tables on Slide 3.22 (32-bit IA-32) and Slide 3.27 (64-bit x86-64): in 32-bit IA-32 mode, which registers can be split into both high (`AH, BH, CH, DH`) and low (`AL, BL, CL, DL`) 8-bit parts, and what 8-bit low sub-registers were added for `RSI`, `RDI`, `RBP`, and `RSP` in x86-64?
options: In IA-32, only EAX, EBX, ECX, and EDX have 8-bit high (AH, BH, CH, DH) and low (AL, BL, CL, DL) parts, while ESI, EDI, EBP, and ESP have only 16-bit names (SI, DI, BP, SP); in x86-64, 8-bit low registers `SIL`, `DIL`, `BPL`, and `SPL` were added alongside 64-bit `RAX..RSP`
In IA-32, ESI and EDI are split into SH/SL and DH/DL
In x86-64, all 8-bit registers were removed
AX is the upper 16 bits of EAX, and AH is the upper 16 bits of RAX
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.22 shows that in 32-bit mode, EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX have 16-bit (AX, BX, CX, DX) and 8-bit high/low (AH/AL, BH/BL, CH/CL, DH/DL) names, whereas ESI, EDI, EBP, ESP have only 16-bit names (SI, DI, BP, SP) for their lower half. Slide 3.27 shows that x86-64 provides 64-bit RAX..RSP and adds 8-bit low names DIL, SIL, BPL, and SPL.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.22 và 3.27: Ở chế độ 32-bit (IA-32), chỉ có EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX mới chia thành nửa 16-bit (AX..DX) và 2 thanh ghi 8-bit cao/thấp (AH/AL..DH/DL), còn ESI, EDI, EBP, ESP chỉ có tên 16-bit thấp (SI, DI, BP, SP). Sang chế độ 64-bit (x86-64), kiến trúc bổ sung thêm các thanh ghi 8-bit thấp `SIL`, `DIL`, `BPL`, `SPL`.

questions.subtopic: FPU (ST0–ST7), MMX, XMM, RSP/RBP & RIP Registers
questions.concept: Floating-Point, MMX, and XMM Registers (Slide 3.26)
questions.question: According to Slide 3.26 ('Floating-Point, MMX, XMM Registers'), what are the bit widths and counts of the x87 Floating-Point data registers (`ST(0)`–`ST(7)`), the MMX registers, and the XMM registers?
options: Sixteen 32-bit floating-point registers; four 16-bit MMX registers; and two 256-bit XMM registers
Eight 80-bit floating-point registers (`ST(0)`–`ST(7)`) arranged as a stack; eight 64-bit MMX registers; and eight 128-bit XMM registers (expanded to 16 in x86-64)
Eight 64-bit floating-point registers; eight 80-bit MMX registers; and eight 32-bit XMM registers
All three register sets are 16 bits wide
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.26 states: Eight 80-bit floating-point data registers ST(0), ST(1), ..., ST(7) arranged as a stack; Eight 64-bit MMX registers used with MMX instructions; Eight 128-bit XMM registers used with SSE instructions (and Slide 6.36 in Ch 6 shows XMM0–XMM15 in 64-bit mode).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.26: Có 8 thanh ghi dấu chấm động 80-bit (`ST(0)` đến `ST(7)`) tổ chức theo kiểu ngăn xếp (stack); 8 thanh ghi MMX 64-bit; và 8 thanh ghi XMM 128-bit dùng cho tập lệnh SSE (mở rộng lên 16 thanh ghi XMM0–XMM15 ở chế độ 64-bit).

questions.subtopic: Status Flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF)
questions.concept: Status Flags in EFLAGS/RFLAGS and their exact bit positions
questions.question: According to the Flag Register (`EFLAGS` / `rFlags`) diagrams and tables on Slides 3.24, 3.25, and 3.32, what are the exact bit numbers and meanings of `CF`, `PF`, `AF`, `ZF`, `SF`, `DF`, and `OF`?
options: CF (bit 7): signed overflow; OF (bit 0): unsigned carry; ZF (bit 1): odd parity
PF (bit 2): set when result is positive; SF (bit 7): set when result is zero

CF (bit 0): unsigned carry/borrow; PF (bit 2): even number of 1s in least-significant byte; AF (bit 4): carry from bit 3 to bit 4; ZF (bit 6): zero result; SF (bit 7): sign bit (1 = negative); DF (bit 10): string direction (increment/decrement); OF (bit 11): signed arithmetic overflow
All status flags occupy bits 24 through 31 of EFLAGS
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.24, 3.25, and 3.32 give both the definitions and exact bit positions: CF = bit 0 (unsigned out of range / carry), PF = bit 2 (even parity in least-significant byte), AF = bit 4 (auxiliary carry from bit 3 to bit 4), ZF = bit 6 (result is zero), SF = bit 7 (copy of sign bit, 1 = negative), DF = bit 10 (direction flag for string operations), and OF = bit 11 (signed arithmetic overflow).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.24, 3.25 và 3.32: `CF` (bit 0: nhớ/mượn không dấu), `PF` (bit 2: chẵn lẻ - bật bằng 1 khi byte thấp nhất có số chẵn các bit 1), `AF` (bit 4: nhớ phụ từ bit 3 sang bit 4), `ZF` (bit 6: kết quả bằng 0), `SF` (bit 7: bit dấu, bằng 1 khi âm), `DF` (bit 10: hướng xử lý chuỗi), và `OF` (bit 11: tràn số có dấu).

questions.concept: Real-Address Mode Logical to 20-Bit Linear/Physical Address Calculation (Slide 3.37 Example)
questions.question: In x86 Real-Address Mode (Slide 3.37), a memory location has a logical address `Segment:Offset = A1F0:04C0` (in hexadecimal). What is the corresponding 20-bit linear (physical) address in hexadecimal?
questions.explanationEn: Using the formula on Slide 3.37: Linear (physical) address = Segment × 10h + Offset. Appending a 0 in hex to `A1F0h` gives `A1F00h`. Adding Offset `04C0h`: `A1F00h + 04C0h = A23C0h`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo ví dụ trên Slide 3.37 (trang 29): Địa chỉ vật lý 20-bit = Segment × 10h + Offset = `A1F00h + 04C0h = A23C0h`.
questions.stepByStep:
1. Multiply Segment A1F0h by 10h (shift left 4 bits): A1F00h.
2. Add Offset 04C0h: A1F00h + 004C0h = A23C0h.

questions.concept: Segment Overlap and Non-Unique Logical Addresses in Real Mode (Slide 3.38)
questions.question: As explained on Slide 3.38 ('Segment Overlap'), a new 64 KB segment starts every `10h` (16) bytes in physical memory, so logical `Segment:Offset` addresses are not unique. Which of the following logical `Segment:Offset` addresses points to the **exact same** 20-bit physical address as `1000:0020` (hex)?
questions.explanationEn: For `1000:0020`, Physical Address = `10000h + 0020h = 10020h`. Checking `1002:0000`: Physical Address = `10020h + 0000h = 10020h` (which is also shown on the right side of Slide 3.38 as 'Start of Segment 2 = 00020' relative to base 00000). Similarly, `1001:0010` also resolves to `10020h`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.38: Địa chỉ vật lý của `1000:0020` là `10000h + 0020h = 10020h`. Địa chỉ logic `1002:0000` cũng có địa chỉ vật lý là `10020h + 0000h = 10020h` (do mỗi đoạn cách nhau 10h = 16 byte nên các đoạn chồng lấp lên nhau).
questions.stepByStep:
1. Compute target physical address: 1000h × 10h + 0020h = 10020h.
2. Evaluate 1002:0000 -> 1002h × 10h + 0000h = 10020h (Match!).

questions.subtopic: Protected Mode Selector, GDT/LDT & Segment Descriptors
questions.concept: Protected Mode Logical-to-Linear Address Translation & Segment Selector Fields
questions.question: In IA-32 Protected Mode (Slides 3.42–3.46), how is a 48-bit logical address (`16-bit Segment Selector` + `32-bit Offset`) translated into a 32-bit Linear Address, and what do the subfields of the 16-bit Segment Selector (`Bits 15:3 Index`, `Bit 2 TI`, `Bits 1:0 RPL`) specify?
options: The 16-bit Segment Selector is multiplied by 10h and added to the 32-bit Offset just like in Real Mode

The upper 13 bits (Index) index into a Segment Descriptor Table selected by Bit 2 `TI` (Table Indicator: `0` = Global Descriptor Table `GDT` pointed to by `GDTR`, `1` = Local Descriptor Table `LDT` pointed to by `LDTR`), while Bits 1:0 specify the Requested Privilege Level (`RPL`); the selected 64-bit Segment Descriptor provides a 32-bit Base Address that is added to the 32-bit Offset to form the 32-bit Linear Address
The Segment Selector directly contains the physical RAM address in bits 15:0
TI = 0 selects the hard disk swap file, and TI = 1 selects the L1 cache
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.42–3.46 explain Protected Mode translation: Logical address = 16-bit Segment Selector + 32-bit Offset. In the 16-bit Selector (Slide 3.43), bits 15–3 are the 13-bit Index into the descriptor table, bit 2 is `TI` (Table Indicator: 0 = GDT, 1 = LDT), and bits 1–0 are `RPL`. The 64-bit Segment Descriptor (loaded into the invisible part of the segment register, Slide 3.46) contains a 32-bit Base Address, 20-bit Limit (in bytes or 4 KB pages, up to 4 GB), and Access Rights. Adding `32-bit Base Address + 32-bit Offset` yields the `32-bit Linear Address`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.42–3.46: Trong Chế độ bảo vệ (Protected Mode), 13 bit cao (bits 15:3) của Segment Selector dùng làm chỉ số (Index) tra vào Bảng mô tả đoạn (Descriptor Table), bit 2 là cờ `TI` (`0` = bảng toàn cục GDT lưu trong GDTR; `1` = bảng cục bộ LDT lưu trong LDTR), 2 bit thấp (1:0) là mức đặc quyền `RPL`. Bộ mô tả đoạn (Segment Descriptor 64-bit) cung cấp Địa chỉ cơ sở (Base Address 32-bit) đem cộng với Offset 32-bit để tạo ra Địa chỉ tuyến tính (Linear Address 32-bit).

questions.subtopic: Paging, Virtual Memory Manager (VMM) & Page Faults
questions.concept: Paging, 4 KB Pages, Virtual Memory Manager, and Page Faults (Slide 3.47)
questions.question: According to Slide 3.47 ('Paging'), how does the IA-32 paging mechanism manage memory, what is the standard page size, and what event is issued by the CPU when a referenced page is not currently in main memory?
options: Paging divides memory into 64 KB overlapping segments; when memory is full, the CPU halts permanently
Paging only operates in 16-bit Real-Address Mode on the 8086

Paging divides the linear address space into fixed-sized 4 KB blocks called pages; the OS Virtual Memory Manager (VMM) uses a Page Directory and Page Tables to map virtual pages to physical frames in RAM or on hard disk; when a referenced page is not in main memory, the CPU issues a Page Fault
A Page Fault occurs whenever an addition results in zero
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.47 states: Paging divides the linear address space into fixed-sized blocks called pages (Intel IA-32 uses 4 KB pages). If main memory is full, pages are stored on the hard disk. The OS Virtual Memory Manager (VMM) uses page tables to map pages and manages loading/unloading. A Page fault is issued by the CPU when a page is not in memory.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.47: Kỹ thuật phân trang (Paging) chia không gian địa chỉ tuyến tính thành các khối kích thước cố định gọi là trang (4 KB trên Intel IA-32). Bộ quản lý bộ nhớ ảo (VMM) của Hệ điều hành dùng bảng trang (page tables) để ánh xạ trang ảo vào RAM hoặc ổ cứng. Khi trang cần truy cập không nằm trong RAM, CPU phát sinh lỗi trang (Page fault).

questions.concept: Real-Mode Physical Address Calculation (1234:5678)
questions.question: In x86 Real-Address Mode, what is the 20-bit linear (physical) address in hexadecimal corresponding to the logical `Segment:Offset` address `1234:5678` (hex)?
questions.explanationEn: Physical Address = Segment × 10h + Offset = 12340h + 5678h = 179B8h.
questions.explanationVi: Địa chỉ vật lý 20-bit = Segment × 10h + Offset = 12340h + 5678h = 179B8h.
questions.stepByStep:
1. Shift Segment 1234h left by 1 hex digit (×10h): 12340h.
2. Add 16-bit Offset 5678h: 12340h + 5678h = 179B8h.

questions.question: In IA-32 Protected Mode (Slides 3.43–3.45), a logical address has a 16-bit Segment Selector `0x0018` and a 32-bit Offset `0x00012340`. options: Descriptor Index = 24, Table = LDT, RPL = 0; Linear Address = 0x00400000
Descriptor Index = 0, Table = GDT, RPL = 3; Linear Address = 0x00012340
Descriptor Index = 3, Table = GDT (TI = 0), RPL = 0; 32-bit Linear Address = 0x00412340
questions.explanationEn: For selector 0x0018 (0000000000011000_2): Bits 15:3 give Index = 3 = 3; Bit 2 is TI = 0 (GDT); Bits 1:0 give RPL = 0. Adding 32-bit Base Address 0x00400000 + 32-bit Offset 0x00012340 = 0x00412340.

questions.concept: Protected Mode Selector Decoding (0x001F) & Linear Address Calculation
questions.question: In IA-32 Protected Mode (Slides 3.43–3.45), a logical address has a 16-bit Segment Selector `0x001F` and a 32-bit Offset `0x0000ABCD`. The selected segment descriptor contains a 32-bit Base Address of `0x7FFF0000`. Decode the Segment Selector `0x001F` (`Index = bits 15:3`, `TI = bit 2`, `RPL = bits 1:0`) and compute the 32-bit Linear Address:
options: Descriptor Index = 31, Table = GDT, RPL = 0; Linear Address = 0x7FFF0000
Descriptor Index = 0, Table = GDT, RPL = 3; Linear Address = 0x0000ABCD
Descriptor Index = 3, Table = LDT (TI = 1), RPL = 3; 32-bit Linear Address = 0x7FFFABCD
questions.explanationEn: For selector 0x001F (0000000000011111_2): Bits 15:3 give Index = 3 = 3; Bit 2 is TI = 1 (LDT); Bits 1:0 give RPL = 3. Adding 32-bit Base Address 0x7FFF0000 + 32-bit Offset 0x0000ABCD = 0x7FFFABCD.
questions.explanationVi: Giải mã Segment Selector `0x001F`: 13 bit cao (15:3) là Index = 3; Bit 2 là TI = 1 (chọn bảng LDT); 2 bit thấp (1:0) là RPL = 3. Địa chỉ tuyến tính 32-bit = Base + Offset = `0x7FFF0000 + 0x0000ABCD = 0x7FFFABCD`.
questions.formula: Index = Selector >> 3; TI = (Selector >> 2) & 1; RPL = Selector & 3; Linear = Base + Offset
questions.stepByStep:
1. Convert 0x001F to binary: 0000000000011111_2.
2. Extract Index = bits[15:3] = 3, TI = bit[2] = 1 (LDT), RPL = bits[1:0] = 3.
3. Compute Linear Address = 0x7FFF0000 + 0x0000ABCD = 0x7FFFABCD.

questions.concept: Protected Mode Selector Decoding (0x0010) & Linear Address Calculation

questions.subtopic: Control Unit, ALU & Internal CPU Bus (Fig 14.2)
questions.concept: Three Main Components of the CPU (Slide 3.9)
questions.question: According to Slide 3.9 ('Main Components of CPU'), how does the Control Unit manage the CPU, and what tasks do the ALU and Registers handle?
options: The Control Unit performs floating-point multiplication; the ALU stores files permanently; Registers cool the motherboard
The Control Unit compiles C code; the ALU manages USB ports; Registers spin the hard disk
All three components are external I/O peripherals

The Control Unit manages the CPU by sending signals like clock, hold, and reset to its parts; the ALU handles arithmetic tasks (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and logical tasks (AND, OR, comparisons); and Registers store data and instructions inside the CPU
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.9 states: Control Unit manages the CPU by sending signals like clock, hold, and reset to its parts; ALU handles arithmetic tasks (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and logical tasks (AND, OR, comparisons); Register is the memory unit that stores data and instructions.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.9: Khối điều khiển (Control Unit) quản lý CPU bằng cách gửi các tín hiệu như clock, hold, reset tới các bộ phận; ALU thực hiện các phép toán số học (cộng, trừ, nhân, chia) và logic (AND, OR, so sánh); còn Thanh ghi (Register) lưu trữ dữ liệu và lệnh trong CPU.

questions.concept: Four Functions of the CPU Instruction Processing Cycle (Slide 3.10)
questions.question: What are the four sequential functions of the CPU when processing instructions from a program (Slide 3.10)?
options: Fetch (retrieve instruction from RAM), Decode (Control Unit interprets fetched instruction), Execute (perform operation using ALU/hardware), and Store (write result back to memory or register)
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.10 defines the four functions of the CPU: Fetch, Decode, Execute, and Store.
questions.explanationVi: Slide 3.10 nêu 4 chức năng tuần tự của CPU khi xử lý lệnh: Fetch (nạp lệnh từ RAM), Decode (giải mã lệnh bởi Control Unit), Execute (thực thi lệnh qua ALU), và Store (lưu kết quả về bộ nhớ hoặc thanh ghi).

questions.concept: CISC vs. RISC Summary in Chapter 4 (Slide 3.19)
questions.question: On Slide 3.19 ('CISC and RISC'), which processor families are cited as canonical examples of CISC versus RISC, and how do their instruction widths and decoding mechanisms compare?
options: CISC (e.g., ARM, MIPS) uses fixed-width instructions; RISC (e.g., Intel x86) uses a microcode interpreter
Both CISC and RISC use variable-width instructions and require software interpreters

CISC (e.g., Intel x86 family) uses a large, complex instruction set with variable-width instructions requiring a microcode interpreter to decode each instruction into a sequence of micro-operations; RISC (e.g., ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC) uses a small, simple instruction set where all instructions have the same width and are decoded and executed directly by hardware
RISC processors have no general-purpose registers
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.19 contrasts CISC (large/complex instruction set, variable width instructions, requires microcode interpreter decoding into micro-operations; Example: Intel x86 family) with RISC (small/simple instruction set, all instructions same width, simpler formats/addressing, decoded and executed directly by hardware; Examples: ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC).
questions.explanationVi: Slide 3.19 đối chiếu CISC (tập lệnh lớn và phức tạp, độ dài lệnh thay đổi, cần bộ thông dịch vi mã thành chuỗi vi thao tác; ví dụ: họ Intel x86) với RISC (tập lệnh nhỏ gọn, mọi lệnh có cùng độ dài, được giải mã và thực thi trực tiếp bằng phần cứng; ví dụ: ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC).

questions.concept: Six 16-Bit Segment Registers in IA-32 (Slides 3.20, 3.23)
questions.question: What are the names and bit widths of the six Segment Registers in the IA-32 architecture (Slides 3.20 and 3.23), and what three distinct types of program contents do segments hold?
options: Six 16-bit segment registers: `CS`, `SS`, `DS`, `ES`, `FS`, and `GS`; they support segmented memory where segments hold Code, Data, and Stack
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.20 and 3.23 show there are six 16-bit Segment Registers (`CS`, `SS`, `DS`, `ES`, `FS`, `GS`) supporting up to six accessible segments at a time containing Code (`CS`), Data (`DS`, `ES`, `FS`, `GS`), and Stack (`SS`).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.20 và 3.23: Có 6 thanh ghi đoạn 16-bit là `CS`, `SS`, `DS`, `ES`, `FS`, `GS` hỗ trợ truy cập tối đa 6 phân đoạn bộ nhớ cùng lúc, chứa Mã lệnh (Code - `CS`), Dữ liệu (Data - `DS, ES, FS, GS`), và Ngăn xếp (Stack - `SS`).

questions.subtopic: FPU (ST0–ST7), MMX, XMM, RSP/RBP & RIP Registers
questions.concept: Roles of RSP, RBP, and RIP in x86-64 (Slides 3.31, 3.33)
questions.question: In the x86-64 architecture (Slides 3.31 and 3.33), why does the top of the stack pointed to by `RSP` have a **low memory address**, what is the rule regarding `RBP`, and how is the `RIP` (Instruction Pointer) register modified?
options: The stack grows upward from address 0; `RIP` can be modified directly using `mov rip, 0`
`RSP` points to the TEXT section, while `RIP` points to the STACK section

Because the x86-64 stack grows downward from high memory toward low memory, `RSP` points to the top (lowest address) of the current function's stack frame; `RBP` is used as a base pointer during function calls and should not be used for general data; `RIP` stores the address (in the TEXT section) of the next instruction and is modified automatically for sequential flow or by jump/call instructions
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.31 shows the stack frame growing from high memory toward low memory, with `RSP` pointing to the top (low address) of the current function's stack frame and `RBP` serving as the base pointer (not to be used for general data). Slide 3.33 states `RIP` stores the location in the TEXT section of the next instruction and changes automatically or via jump instructions.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.31 và 3.33: Ngăn xếp (Stack) phát triển từ địa chỉ cao xuống địa chỉ thấp nên `RSP` chứa địa chỉ đỉnh stack (địa chỉ thấp) của khung hàm hiện tại; `RBP` làm con trỏ cơ sở (base pointer) khi gọi hàm; còn `RIP` trỏ tới lệnh kế tiếp trong vùng TEXT và tự động thay đổi tuần tự hoặc qua các lệnh nhảy (jump).

questions.subtopic: Status Flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF)
questions.concept: Evaluating Parity Flag (PF) and Auxiliary Carry Flag (AF) (Slide 3.25)
questions.question: Suppose an 8-bit addition `0000 1001_2 (9) + 0000 1010_2 (10)` produces the result `0001 0011_2 (19)`. Based on the Status Flag rules on Slide 3.25 (`AF = 1` when there is a carry from bit 3 to bit 4; `PF = 1` when the least-significant byte contains an even number of `1` bits), what are the values of `AF`, `PF`, `ZF`, and `SF`?
options: AF = 1 (carry from bit 3 to bit 4), PF = 0 (since 00010011_2 has three '1' bits, which is odd), ZF = 0, SF = 0
questions.explanationEn: Adding lower nibbles: `1001_2 (9) + 1010_2 (10) = 1_0011_2 (19)`, which generates a carry out of bit 3 into bit 4, so `AF = 1`. The 8-bit result `0001 0011_2` has three `1` bits (bits 4, 1, 0); since 3 is odd, the even-parity flag is `PF = 0`. Since result != 0 and bit 7 is 0, `ZF = 0` and `SF = 0`.
questions.explanationVi: Khi cộng 4 bit thấp: `1001_2 (9) + 1010_2 (10) = 1_0011_2`, có bit nhớ truyền từ bit 3 sang bit 4 nên cờ nhớ phụ `AF = 1`. Kết quả `0001 0011_2` có 3 bit `1` (số lẻ) nên cờ chẵn lẻ `PF = 0`. Kết quả khác 0 và bit dấu (bit 7) bằng 0 nên `ZF = 0, SF = 0`.
questions.stepByStep:
1. Add low nibbles: 9 + 10 = 19 = 16 + 3 -> carry from bit 3 to bit 4 -> AF = 1.
2. Count 1-bits in 00010011_2: three 1s (odd) -> PF = 0.
3. Result is non-zero (ZF=0) and MSB=0 (SF=0).

questions.subtopic: Control Flag (DF) & System Flags (TF, IF, IOPL, VM)
questions.concept: Control Flag (DF) and System Flags in EFLAGS (Slide 3.24)
questions.question: In the `EFLAGS` register diagram on Slide 3.24 (p. 19), which flag is the sole **Control Flag** (and what does it control), and which flags belong to the **System Flags** group?
options: `CF` is the Control Flag; `AF` and `PF` are the System Flags
`ZF` is the Control Flag; `EAX` and `EBX` are the System Flags
There are no System Flags in the EFLAGS register

`DF` (Direction Flag) is the Control Flag (controlling increment/decrement direction for string operations); System Flags include `TF` (Trap flag), `IF` (Interrupt flag), `IOPL` (I/O privilege level), `NT` (Nested task), `RF` (Resume flag), `VM` (Virtual 8086 mode), `AC` (Alignment check), `VIF`, `VIP`, and `ID`
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.24 categorizes EFLAGS into three columns: Status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF), Control flags (DF = Direction flag), and System flags (TF, IF, IOPL, NT, RF, VM, AC, VIF, VIP, ID).
questions.explanationVi: Slide 3.24 chia các cờ trong EFLAGS thành 3 nhóm: Cờ trạng thái (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF), Cờ điều khiển (`DF` - Direction flag điều khiển hướng tăng/giảm cho lệnh chuỗi), và Cờ hệ thống (`TF, IF, IOPL, NT, RF, VM, AC, VIF, VIP, ID`).

questions.subtopic: Code, Data & Stack Segments (CS, DS, SS, ES/FS/GS)
questions.concept: Why Memory Segmentation is Necessary in 16-bit x86 and Segment Size (Slide 3.34)
questions.question: Why was memory segmentation necessary on the 16-bit x86 architecture (Slide 3.34), and what is the maximum size of a single memory segment in Real-Address Mode?
options: Because 16-bit registers can hold 4 GB addresses without segmentation

Because a 20-bit physical memory address (1 MB) cannot fit into a single 16-bit CPU register; since registers are 16 bits wide, each segment spans 2^16 = 65,536 (64K) bytes/locations (offsets 0000h to FFFFh)
Each segment in Real Mode is 16 MB in size
Segmentation was invented only to slow down the ALU
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.34 explains: 'Memory segmentation is necessary since the 20-bits memory addresses can not fit in the 16-bits CPU registers. Since x86 registers are 16-bits wide, a memory segment is made of 2^16 consecutive words/bytes (i.e. 64K), starting with 0000 up to FFFF (hex).'
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.34: Phân đoạn bộ nhớ (Memory segmentation) là cần thiết vì địa chỉ vật lý 20-bit (1 MB) không thể chứa vừa trong một thanh ghi 16-bit. Với độ lệch Offset 16-bit (`0000h` đến `FFFFh`), mỗi đoạn có kích thước tối đa là 2^16 = 64 KB.

questions.subtopic: Code, Data & Stack Segments (CS, DS, SS, ES/FS/GS)
questions.concept: Program Segments: Code, Data, and Stack Registers (Slide 3.35)
questions.question: According to Slide 3.35 ('Program Segments'), how is the Stack segment organized, what is it used for, and which segment registers hold the segment numbers for the Code, Data, and Stack segments?
options: The Stack is a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue stored in `CS`; Code is stored in `SS`

The Stack is a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) buffer used to implement procedure calls and temporarily hold addresses and data; segment numbers for Code, Data, and Stack are stored in `CS`, `DS`, and `SS`, respectively
Code, Data, and Stack must all be stored in the `EFLAGS` register
A program segment must always occupy all 64K locations even if the program is 10 bytes long
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.35 states that the Stack is a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) buffer used for procedure calls and temporary storage of addresses/data, and the segment numbers for Code, Data, and Stack are stored in `CS`, `DS`, and `SS`, respectively.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.35: Ngăn xếp (Stack) có cấu trúc vào sau ra trước (LIFO) dùng để gọi thủ tục và lưu tạm địa chỉ/dữ liệu. Số hiệu đoạn của vùng Mã lệnh (Code), Dữ liệu (Data) và Ngăn xếp (Stack) được lưu tương ứng trong các thanh ghi `CS`, `DS` và `SS`.

questions.concept: Flat Memory Model and .MODEL flat Directive (Slides 3.39, 3.41)
questions.question: In modern 32-bit operating systems using the **Flat Memory Model** (`.MODEL flat`, Slides 3.39 and 3.41), how are the segment registers (`CS, DS, SS, ES`) configured and what is their base address?
options: Each segment is restricted to 64 KB with a different random base address

All segments are mapped by the operating system to the same 32-bit linear address space (up to 2^32 = 4 GB) with `base address = 0` for all segments, and the OS maps linear (virtual) addresses onto physical addresses using paging
The `.MODEL flat` directive switches the CPU into 16-bit MS-DOS Real Mode
The Flat Memory Model disables paging and virtual memory
questions.explanationEn: Slides 3.39 and 3.41 explain that in the Flat Memory Model (`.MODEL flat`), segmentation is effectively turned off by mapping all segments (`CS, DS, SS, ES`) to the same 32-bit linear address space (up to 4 GB) with `base address = 0 for all segments`, while the OS maps linear/virtual addresses to physical addresses via paging.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.39 và 3.41: Trong Mô hình bộ nhớ phẳng (Flat Memory Model, khai báo bằng chỉ thị `.MODEL flat`), mọi thanh ghi đoạn (`CS, DS, SS, ES`) đều được Hệ điều hành ánh xạ vào cùng một không gian địa chỉ tuyến tính 32-bit (tối đa 4 GB) với địa chỉ cơ sở `base address = 0`, kết hợp kỹ thuật phân trang (paging).

questions.subtopic: Protected Mode Selector, GDT/LDT & Segment Descriptors
questions.concept: Global Descriptor Table (GDT) vs. Local Descriptor Table (LDT) (Slide 3.44)
questions.question: According to Slide 3.44 ('Segment Descriptor Tables'), how do the Global Descriptor Table (GDT) and Local Descriptor Table (LDT) differ, and which registers store their memory addresses?
options: Only one GDT is provided by the OS (initialized at boot up, containing descriptors for all programs and the OS itself, with its address stored in `GDTR`); an LDT can be uniquely assigned per program (containing descriptors for only one program, with its address stored in `LDTR`), though modern OSes like Windows XP use one GDT table
Every program has 10 GDTs stored in `EAX`; the OS has no GDT
The GDT is stored on CD-ROM; the LDT is stored in the ALU shifter
GDTR and LDTR are 8-bit status flags inside EFLAGS
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.44 states: Only one GDT table is provided by the OS (initialized during boot up, holds segment descriptors for all programs and the OS itself, address stored in `GDTR`; modern OSes like Windows-XP use one GDT). An LDT can be unique per program, with its address stored in `LDTR`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.44: Toàn hệ thống chỉ có một Bảng mô tả toàn cục (GDT) duy nhất do Hệ điều hành khởi tạo lúc boot và lưu địa chỉ trong thanh ghi `GDTR`. Bảng mô tả cục bộ (LDT) có thể cấp riêng cho từng chương trình và lưu địa chỉ trong thanh ghi `LDTR`.

questions.subtopic: Protected Mode Selector, GDT/LDT & Segment Descriptors
questions.concept: Segment Descriptor Limit and Granularity (Slide 3.45)
questions.question: In a Protected Mode Segment Descriptor (Slide 3.45), the **Segment Limit** field is a `20-bit` number (`2^20 = 1,048,576`) that specifies the size of the segment. Since 20 bits can directly count up to `1 MB` in single bytes, how does IA-32 allow a segment size to reach up to `4 GB`?
options: The size can be specified either in single bytes or in multiples of `4 KB pages` (`2^12` bytes); using 4 KB page granularity, a 20-bit limit specifies up to `2^20 × 4 KB = 2^32 bytes = 4 GB`
The CPU multiplies the 20-bit limit by 10h as in Real Mode to get 16 MB
The Segment Limit field is actually 64 bits wide in IA-32
A segment in Protected Mode can never exceed 64 KB
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.45 states: 'Segment Limit: 20-bit number that specifies the size of the segment. The size is specified either in bytes or multiple of 4 KB pages. Using 4 KB pages, segment size can range from 4 KB to 4 GB (2^20 × 4 KB = 4 GB).'
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.45: Trường Segment Limit dài 20-bit. Kích thước đoạn có thể tính theo đơn vị byte hoặc theo bội số của trang `4 KB` (4 KB pages). Khi dùng đơn vị trang 4 KB, kích thước đoạn tối đa đạt `2^20 × 4 KB = 4 GB`.
questions.stepByStep:
1. 20-bit limit provides 2^20 = 1,048,576 units.
2. With 4 KB (2^12 B) page granularity: 2^20 × 2^12 B = 2^32 B = 4 GB.

questions.subtopic: Protected Mode Selector, GDT/LDT & Segment Descriptors
questions.concept: Visible and Invisible Parts of a Segment Register in Protected Mode (Slide 3.46)
questions.question: According to Slide 3.46 ('Segment Visible and Invisible Parts'), why does each segment register (`CS, SS, DS, ES, FS, GS`) have both a **Visible part** and an **Invisible part** (Descriptor Cache) in Protected Mode, and what are their sizes?
options: The Visible part is 64 bits and the Invisible part is 8 bits
The Invisible part stores the user's password in BIOS ROM
Only CS has an invisible part; DS and SS do not

The Visible part is the 16-bit Segment Register (holding the Segment Selector visible to the programmer); the Invisible part is a 64-bit shadow register holding the Segment Descriptor (base address, size/limit, access rights) automatically loaded from the descriptor table so the CPU does not have to access the GDT/LDT in memory on every memory reference
questions.explanationEn: Slide 3.46 shows that each segment register has a 16-bit Visible part (Segment selector, visible to the programmer) and a 64-bit Invisible part (Segment Descriptor containing Segment base address, size, access rights, etc., automatically loaded from the descriptor table).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 3.46: Trong Protected Mode, mỗi thanh ghi đoạn có Phần nhìn thấy được (Visible part = 16-bit Segment Selector) và Phần ẩn (Invisible part = 64-bit Segment Descriptor chứa địa chỉ cơ sở, giới hạn kích thước, quyền truy cập được nạp tự động từ bảng mô tả) giúp tăng tốc dịch địa chỉ.

questions.subtopic: Paging, Virtual Memory Manager (VMM) & Page Faults
questions.concept: Calculating Number of 4 KB Pages in a 32-Bit Linear Address Space
questions.question: In Intel IA-32 Protected Mode with Paging enabled (Slide 3.47), the linear (virtual) address space of a program is `32 bits` (`2^32 = 4 GB`) and is divided into fixed-sized pages of `4 KB` (`2^12 = 4,096 bytes`). How many bits of the 32-bit linear address represent the byte offset within a 4 KB page, and how many total 4 KB pages exist in the 4 GB linear address space?
options: 16 bits for the page offset; 65,536 (64K) pages total
10 bits for the page offset; 4,194,304 (4M) pages total
12 bits for the page offset (`2^12 = 4,096`); the upper 20 bits identify `2^20 = 1,048,576` (1M) pages in the 4 GB address space
20 bits for the page offset; 4,096 (4K) pages total
questions.explanationEn: Since each page is 4 KB = 2^12 bytes, the lower 12 bits of the 32-bit linear address specify the offset within the page. The remaining 32 - 12 = 20 bits specify the virtual page number, yielding 2^20 = 1,048,576 (1M) pages of 4 KB each (2^20 × 4 KB = 4 GB).
questions.explanationVi: Vì mỗi trang có kích thước `4 KB = 2^12 bytes`, 12 bit thấp của địa chỉ tuyến tính 32-bit dùng làm độ lệch (offset) trong trang, và 20 bit cao xác định số hiệu trang, tương ứng với `2^20 = 1,048,576` (1M) trang trong không gian 4 GB.
questions.stepByStep:
1. Page size = 4 KB = 4096 bytes = 2^12 bytes -> 12-bit offset.
2. Total pages = 2^32 bytes / 2^12 bytes/page = 2^20 = 1,048,576 pages.
